A physicist is a scientist who studies physics — the branch of science that tries to understand the most fundamental rules of how the universe works. This includes understanding matter (what things are made of), energy (what makes things move or change), space, time, and the forces that govern everything from the tiniest subatomic particles to the largest galaxies.

In the simplest terms: if you want to understand why the universe behaves the way it does at its deepest level, you become a physicist.
What Makes Physics Different from Other Sciences?

To understand what a physicist does, it helps to first understand what makes physics physics.

  • A biologist studies living things.
  • A chemist studies how substances interact and transform.
  • A geologist studies the Earth.

But a physicist studies the underlying rules that govern all of these — the fundamental laws that make chemistry possible, that make life possible, that make the Earth exist at all. Physics is the most foundational of the natural sciences. Everything else, in some sense, is built on top of it.

For example, a chemist studies how hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. A physicist wants to know why atoms bond the way they do — what forces are acting, what energy is exchanged, and what mathematical laws describe it all.
What Does a Physicist Actually Do?

A physicist's job is to ask deep questions about nature and then find precise, testable answers.

Their work typically involves:

1. Observing and asking questions
A physicist notices something about the natural world and asks: Why does this happen? What rule is behind this? For example: Why does light bend when it passes through glass? Why do objects fall at the same rate regardless of weight?

2. Building theories
A physicist develops a theory — a logical, mathematical explanation for what they've observed. This is not a "guess." In science, a theory is a well-structured explanation backed by evidence. Physicists use mathematics as their primary language because math is precise and universal.

3. Running experiments
A physicist (or a team) designs experiments to test whether their theory is correct. They measure, collect data, and check whether the real world matches their prediction. If it doesn't, the theory needs to be revised or discarded.

4. Revising understanding
When experiments reveal something unexpected, physicists revise old theories or build new ones. This is how science progresses. For instance, Isaac Newton's laws of motion were considered complete for centuries — until Albert Einstein showed that at very high speeds or in strong gravitational fields, Newton's model breaks down and a better model (General Relativity) is needed.
The Two Broad Types of Physicists

Physicists generally fall into one of two broad categories:

1. Theoretical Physicists
These physicists work primarily with mathematics and logic. They develop theories and models to explain physical phenomena. They may work at a desk or a chalkboard, using equations to describe how the universe should behave. They don't necessarily run experiments themselves — they produce ideas that experimentalists then test.

Example: Albert Einstein was largely a theoretical physicist. He developed the theory of relativity through thought experiments and mathematics, not laboratory experiments.

2. Experimental Physicists
These physicists design and conduct real-world experiments to observe physical phenomena, test theories, and measure things with precision. They work in laboratories with sophisticated instruments, particle accelerators, telescopes, and detectors.

Example: The scientists at CERN who discovered the Higgs boson in 2012 were experimental physicists.

In practice, many physicists fall somewhere in between, and the two types work closely together. A theorist might predict the existence of a new particle; an experimentalist then builds the equipment to find it.
The Main Branches of Physics (and the Physicists Who Work in Them)

Physics is a vast field. Physicists often specialize in one particular area:

Classical Mechanics — Studies the motion of everyday objects: how a ball rolls, how a bridge holds weight, how a planet orbits a star. This is the physics of Newton.

Thermodynamics — Studies heat, temperature, and energy transfer. Why does a hot cup of coffee cool down? How do engines work?

Electromagnetism — Studies electricity, magnetism, and light. These are actually different aspects of the same underlying force. Your phone, your computer, all modern electronics — rooted in this.

Quantum Mechanics — Studies the behavior of matter and energy at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles (electrons, protons, photons). At this scale, the universe behaves in strange, counterintuitive ways — particles can exist in multiple states at once, and you can only speak of probabilities, not certainties.

Relativity — Einstein's framework describing how space, time, gravity, and motion work at very high speeds or in intense gravitational fields. GPS satellites require corrections based on relativity to work accurately.

Particle Physics — Studies the most fundamental building blocks of matter: quarks, leptons, bosons, and the forces between them. Particle physicists use enormous machines called particle accelerators (like CERN's Large Hadron Collider) to smash particles together at near-light speed and observe what results.

Astrophysics and Cosmology — Applies physics to understand stars, galaxies, black holes, dark matter, dark energy, and the origin and evolution of the universe. Cosmologists ask: How did the universe begin? How will it end?

Condensed Matter Physics — Studies the properties of solid and liquid matter — why some materials conduct electricity, why others are magnetic, how superconductors work. This is actually the largest single branch of physics in terms of active researchers.

Nuclear Physics — Studies the nucleus of the atom — its structure, how it releases energy (nuclear fission and fusion), and how radioactive decay works.

Optics — Studies the behavior of light — how it travels, bends, reflects, and interacts with matter. Lasers, optical fibers, cameras all come from this.

Biophysics — Applies the methods and principles of physics to understand biological systems — how proteins fold, how nerves conduct signals, how DNA is packed inside a cell.

Geophysics and Atmospheric Physics — Applies physics to study the Earth's structure, earthquakes, ocean currents, and the atmosphere (including climate science).

A physicist working in any of these areas is still called a physicist — they may sometimes be called by more specific names (astrophysicist, nuclear physicist, etc.), but "physicist" remains the general term.
How Does Someone Become a Physicist?

Becoming a physicist requires serious, sustained education in both physics and mathematics.

  • Undergraduate degree in physics (or a closely related field like mathematics or engineering physics). This typically takes 3–4 years.
  • Postgraduate degree — most research physicists go on to complete a Master's degree and then a PhD (Doctorate) in physics. A PhD typically takes 4–6 years and involves original research — the student must discover or contribute something genuinely new to the field.
  • After the PhD, many physicists do one or more postdoctoral positions — essentially research jobs under the supervision of a senior scientist — before getting an independent research position.

Not every physicist follows this exact path, and not every physicist works in academic research (see below), but a PhD is the standard credential for those who want to do original scientific research.
Where Do Physicists Work?

Physicists work in a variety of settings:

Universities and research institutions — This is where most academic physicists work. They conduct research and teach students. Well-known research institutions include MIT, Caltech, CERN, Fermilab, and the Max Planck Institutes.

Government laboratories — Many countries fund national laboratories where physicists work on both pure research and applied problems. Examples: NASA, ISRO, the national laboratories in the US (Argonne, Oak Ridge, Lawrence Berkeley, etc.).

Private industry and technology companies — Physicists are highly valued in industries like semiconductors, telecommunications, medical devices, aerospace, energy, and finance (quantitative analysis). Companies like Intel, IBM, Lockheed Martin, and many others employ physicists.

Medical and healthcare sectors — Medical physicists work in hospitals and clinics, ensuring that radiation-based treatments (like radiotherapy for cancer) and imaging technologies (like MRI and CT scans) are used safely and effectively.

Finance — A surprising number of physicists work in finance and economics, applying their mathematical modeling skills to financial markets. They are sometimes called "quants" (quantitative analysts).
What Has Physics (and Physicists) Given the World?

It's worth pausing to appreciate the scale of what physicists have contributed to human life. Many technologies we take for granted exist because physicists asked deep, abstract questions that, at the time, seemed to have no practical use:

  • Electricity and modern electronics — from the work of physicists like Faraday, Maxwell, and later quantum physicists who explained semiconductors, leading to transistors, microchips, and all of modern computing.
  • Nuclear energy and nuclear medicine — from nuclear physics.
  • Lasers — from quantum mechanics. Used in surgery, manufacturing, communications, barcode scanners, and countless other applications.
  • MRI scanners — from nuclear magnetic resonance physics.
  • GPS — requires corrections based on both Special and General Relativity to function accurately.
  • The internet — emerged partly from tools built for physicists (the World Wide Web was invented at CERN).
  • Solar panels — based on the photoelectric effect, explained by Einstein.
How Is a Physicist Different from Similar Roles?

It's easy to confuse "physicist" with related terms:

Physicist vs. Chemist — Both study matter, but a chemist focuses on the properties and reactions of chemical substances (molecules and compounds), while a physicist is more concerned with the fundamental laws underlying all matter and energy. Physics and chemistry overlap significantly (in fields like physical chemistry and quantum chemistry), but the physicist typically goes deeper into fundamental principles.

Physicist vs. Engineer — An engineer applies scientific knowledge to build things — bridges, circuits, machines, software. A physicist discovers and explains scientific knowledge. Engineers often use the laws that physicists discovered. In practice, the boundary blurs: some physicists do very applied work, and some engineers work on very fundamental problems.

Physicist vs. Mathematician — A mathematician works in pure logic and abstract structures, without necessarily caring whether their work describes the physical world. A physicist uses mathematics as a tool to describe nature, and ultimately tests their ideas against reality. However, many areas of mathematics were developed by or alongside physics (calculus was co-invented by Newton to solve physics problems), and some theoretical physicists work in ways that closely resemble mathematics.

Physicist vs. Astronomer — An astronomer observes and studies celestial objects — stars, planets, galaxies. An astrophysicist applies the laws of physics to explain why those objects behave as they do. Today, the line between astronomy and astrophysics is very thin, and most astronomers are also astrophysicists. But "physicist" is the broader category.
A Few Famous Physicists, and Why They Matter

To make the concept vivid:

  • Isaac Newton — Formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation. Explained why planets orbit the sun and why objects fall.
  • James Clerk Maxwell — Unified electricity and magnetism into a single theory of electromagnetism. Predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves (light is one of them).
  • Marie Curie — Pioneered research on radioactivity. The first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics and Chemistry).
  • Albert Einstein — Developed the Special and General Theories of Relativity. Explained the photoelectric effect (which earned him the Nobel Prize). Transformed our understanding of space, time, gravity, and energy.
  • Niels Bohr — One of the founders of quantum mechanics. Developed the first model of the atom that incorporated quantum ideas.
  • Richard Feynman — Made major contributions to quantum electrodynamics (QED). Also famous for making physics deeply accessible to non-scientists.
  • Stephen Hawking — Worked on black holes, cosmology, and the nature of time. Showed that black holes can emit radiation (now called Hawking radiation).
  • C. V. Raman — Indian physicist who discovered the Raman Effect (how light scatters through matter), for which he won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930. The first Asian to win a Nobel in science.
Summary

A physicist is a scientist who studies the fundamental laws of nature — the deepest rules that govern matter, energy, space, and time. They ask the most foundational questions about why the universe is the way it is, build mathematical theories to explain what they observe, and test those theories through experiments. Physicists can be theoretical (working with math and ideas) or experimental (working in labs), and they specialize in areas ranging from quantum mechanics to cosmology to condensed matter. Their work underpins much of modern technology and our understanding of the cosmos. Becoming a physicist typically requires advanced university education, usually up to a PhD. They work in universities, research labs, industry, medicine, and even finance.

In one sentence: a physicist is someone who professionally studies the fundamental rules of how the universe works.
